## Week 1
#### Readings
* [Chapple (2017) "Income Inequality and Urban Displacement: The New Gentrification"](https://escholarship.org/uc/item/6rb5b8bd) (10 pp.) — the argument that frames the course: focus on *displacement*, not just gentrification, and treat it as an *income* crisis, not only a housing one.

#### Tuesday July 7 - Lecture
* Course introduction and [syllabus](syllabus.qmd)
* How to use AI in this course - discussion and live demo

#### Thursday July 9 - Lab
* Lab 1: getting started in RStudio on the DataHub (we walk through it together online), intro to R, and your first Census number
* AI tutorial: debugging with AI, verifying answers, and sharing your conversation link

#### Set up this week
* Get a free census API key at <https://api.census.gov/data/key_signup.html> (a couple minutes). The key arrives by email — **click the activation link in that email**, or the key won't work in lab.
* Set up a free account on an AI assistant that can share a public conversation link (Perplexity recommended; ChatGPT, Gemini, or Claude also work). Sign in with a **personal** account, not your CalNet login, so that link-sharing works. [See the AI policy for details.](syllabus.html#ai-policy)

## Week 2

#### Readings
***Due Thursday July 16***

* [Walker (2023) “Analyzing US Census Data: Methods, Maps, and Models in R”: Preface, Ch 1, & Ch 2](https://walker-data.com/census-r/index.html)

*Optional deeper dive on the Week 1 Chapple reading:* [Zuk et al. (2015) "Gentrification, Displacement and the Role of Public Investment: A Literature Review"](https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Karen-Chapple/publication/334638363_Gentrification_Displacement_and_the_Role_of_Public_Investment_A_Literature_Review/links/5d37697f4585153e591c453f/Gentrification-Displacement-and-the-Role-of-Public-Investment-A-Literature-Review.pdf)

#### Tuesday July 14 - Lecture

* How a move happens: the mobility curve — hard displacement, soft displacement, and being stuck
* Why the map has a race: 130 years of segregation in four periods
* Where precarity lands now: the post-pandemic era

#### Thursday July 16 - Lab

* Lab 2: finding the data you need — income, race, and place (`code/lab2_census_data.R` on the [DataHub](https://r.datahub.berkeley.edu/hub/user-redirect/git-pull?repo=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fevictionresearch%2FSOC-N100-Housing-Precarity-2026&urlpath=rstudio%2F))
* Search the ACS variable catalog yourself, build HUD's income tiers with `mutate()`, compare incomes across race, and build your first ggplot chart — rebuilding two of Tuesday's charts from live Census data
* If you missed lab 1: get your free Census API key first (see the Week 1 setup steps above) — you'll need it tonight

## Week 3
#### Readings
***Due before lab, Thursday July 23***

* [Walker (2023) Chapter 3](https://walker-data.com/census-r/wrangling-census-data-with-tidyverse-tools.html) & [Chapter 4](https://walker-data.com/census-r/exploring-us-census-data-with-visualization.html) — chapter 3 is lab 3's wrangling verbs (filter/mutate/group_by, margins of error); chapter 4 is its charts. Read them behind the lab and everything clicks twice.

#### Tuesday July 21 - Lab

* Warm-up tour in [Social Explorer](https://www.socialexplorer.com/): how census geographies nest — states, counties, tracts, block groups, blocks — and what size each polygon really is
* Lab 3, part A: building your first real measure — the share of renters who are rent-burdened (`code/lab3_rent_burden.R` on the [DataHub](https://r.datahub.berkeley.edu/hub/user-redirect/git-pull?repo=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fevictionresearch%2FSOC-N100-Housing-Precarity-2026&urlpath=rstudio%2F))
* Reading Census tables like a researcher: dollars vs. counts and the universe rule, hunting down table B25070 in the catalog yourself, census-tract neighborhoods, and reshaping with `pivot_wider()` — the skills Assignment 2's build-a-measure asks for

#### Thursday July 23 - Lab

* Lab 3, part B — picking up at section 7: charts, done right. Which plot answers which question — bar, histogram, boxplot, scatter, and the chart-picker card — with the [ggplot2 cheat sheet](https://opensource.posit.co/resources/cheatsheets/data-visualization/) at your elbow, plus summarizing with `group_by()` + `summarize()`
* Your turn: rebuild the measure and charts for your own county (the seed of Assignment 1 and beyond)
* Walkthrough of the Assignment 1 model answer (`code/a1_example.R`) — A1 is due Monday July 27
* Optional after-class extras: the burden over time (write your first function and `map()` it across years), and who carries the burden — rent-burden rates by household income group, built from the same Census table (B25074) the Eviction Research Network's own models pull

#### **Assignment 1** - *Due Monday, July 27 @5pm*

A short solo warm-up, and the first step of a thread you carry through Assignment 2 and your final project. Pick a county, set of counties, or region you care about - you will keep working with this same area all term.

1. Use `get_acs()` to pull one ACS variable that says something about housing precarity (for example, rent burden, median rent, or the share of households that rent).
2. Make one chart of it (a bar chart across your counties works well).
3. Write two or three sentences describing what the chart shows and anything that surprised you.

Submit your R script, the chart, your sentences, and the share link(s) to any AI you used. Keep it simple - no bibliography or ASA formatting needed yet. Submit to bCourses.

## Week 4

#### Readings

***Due Thursday July 30***
[Walker (2023) Chapter 5, sections 5.1–5.2](https://walker-data.com/census-r/census-geographic-data-and-applications-in-r.html) and [Chapter 6, sections 6.1–6.3](https://walker-data.com/census-r/mapping-census-data-with-r.html) — the simple core of Census mapping: what the shapes are, then choropleth maps with `geom_sf` and `tmap` (the tool lab 4 uses). The rest of both chapters is optional reference — skip the coordinate-system math (§5.4) and the advanced maps (§6.6) unless you're curious.

#### Tuesday July 28 - Lab

* Lab 4, part A: real eviction records — load ERN's Indiana court-filing data, compute eviction rates, and make your first joins to Census data (`code/lab4_evictions_mapping.R` on the [DataHub](https://r.datahub.berkeley.edu/hub/user-redirect/git-pull?repo=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fevictionresearch%2FSOC-N100-Housing-Precarity-2026&urlpath=rstudio%2F))
* Hard displacement meets lab 3's soft-displacement measures

#### Thursday July 30 - Lab

* Lab 4, part B: put eviction rates on maps
* [Review San Diego Displacement Study](https://urban-displacement.github.io/edr-sandag/)

## Week 5

#### **Assignment 2** - *Due Monday, August 3 @5pm*

Build directly on Assignment 1: stay with the same area and go deeper. This becomes the seed of your final group project.

Add two or three more ACS variables and combine them into a measure of displacement risk, inequality, or some other housing precarity measure using the American Community Survey. Include descriptive statistics, plots, and an interpretation of what you found. End with a draft research question and at least two hypotheses you could test about the disparate impact of displacement in your area. Submit to bCourses.

For this assignment you will submit:

1. R code script that is replicable by the grader,

2. a brief writeup explaining your assignment with plots and context,
    * Include one or more introductory paragraphs summarizing what you are analyzing and your overall findings.
    * Text and plots walking the reader through a more detailed understanding of what you found. Make sure to describe your plots.
    * A draft research question and at least two hypotheses for your final project.

3. Bibliography and inline citations in ASA (American Sociological Association) format.

4. List of URL links to any and all AI usage (use any approved AI tool that can share a public conversation link).
    * In your code, put the URL in comments next to the relevant area.
    * In your writeup, put the URL in footnotes near the section or text in which you used AI. [See AI policy in the Syllabus for more info.](syllabus.html#ai-policy)


These assignments will be graded on the [scale in the syllabus](syllabus.html#course-grading). This grade is to help you see the quality of your work but the final grade will be graded as complete or incomplete. No late assignments will be accepted except for special accommodations. You can volunteer to present a 5-minute demo of your assignment in class.

#### Readings

***Due Tuesday August 4***
[Bates (2013) "Gentrification and Displacement Study: Implementing an Equitable Inclusive Development Strategy in the Context of Gentrification"](https://www.portland.gov/sites/default/files/2020-01/2-gentrification-and-displacement-study-05.18.13.pdf)

*Optional, for Thursday's segregation lab:* [Walker (2023) section 8.1, "Indices of segregation and diversity"](https://walker-data.com/census-r/modeling-us-census-data.html) — just that section; the rest of chapter 8 (regression and machine learning) is beyond our scope.

#### Tuesday August 4 - Lecture

* Form randomly assigned groups of 2 or 3 and discussion on final group project
* Draft some ideas on your final group project
    * Include what area you want to study (at least two counties or a region),
    * what you want to explore about displacement (at least 3-5 different data points/plots),
    * what data you will use to capture this.
* Present your idea to the group and get a sign-off from Tim

#### Thursday August 6 - Lab

* Bonus lab: working with data under memory constraints (`code/lab6_bonus_memory.R` on the [DataHub](https://r.datahub.berkeley.edu/hub/user-redirect/git-pull?repo=https%3A%2F%2Fgithub.com%2Fevictionresearch%2FSOC-N100-Housing-Precarity-2026&urlpath=rstudio%2F)) - the survival kit for your final project: watching your memory budget, dropping geometry, chunking big Census pulls, caching with saveRDS, and querying bigger-than-memory parquet data with duckdb + arrow
